stem.text: A delivery drone flies over a park. Its altitude above the ground is \( A(t) \) meters, where \( t \) is measured in minutes, and \( A \) is differentiable for \( 0 \le t \le 12 \). Selected values of \( A(t) \) are given in the table. \[ \begin{array}{c|ccccc} t \text{ (minutes)} & 0 & 3 & 5 & 9 & 12 \\ \hline A(t) \text{ (meters)} & 20 & 50 & 62 & 90 & 62 \end{array} \] A second drone has altitude \( H(t) = 50 - 4\left|t - 5\right| \) meters for \( 0 \le t \le 10 \).

parts.prompt: Find the average rate of change of \( A \) over the interval \( 0 \le t \le 12 \). Show the computation that leads to your answer.

points.criterion: Writes (A(12) - A(0))/(12 - 0) with the table values, (62 - 20)/12, and gives 7/2. The unsimplified quotient 42/12 and the decimal 3.5 are accepted.

parts.prompt: Must there be a time \( t \), with \( 3 < t < 5 \), at which \( A'(t) = 6 \)? Must there be a time \( t \), with \( 9 < t < 12 \), at which \( A'(t) = -\frac{28}{3} \)? Justify each answer.

worked_solution.text: Average rate of change over 3 <= t <= 5.
A is differentiable, so it is continuous on 3 <= t <= 5 and differentiable on 3 < t < 5. By the Mean Value Theorem there is such a time.
Average rate of change over 9 <= t <= 12.
The same hypotheses hold on 9 <= t <= 12, so the Mean Value Theorem gives such a time.

points.criterion: Shows the average rate of change of A over 3 <= t <= 5 as a difference quotient with values, (62 - 50)/(5 - 3), equal to 6. The bare value 6 with no quotient does not earn the point.

Answers yes for 3 < t < 5, stating that A is differentiable (so continuous on 3 <= t <= 5 and differentiable on 3 < t < 5) and invoking the Mean Value Theorem. An appeal to the Intermediate Value Theorem does not earn the point.
Shows the average rate of change of A over 9 <= t <= 12 as a difference quotient with values, (62 - 90)/(12 - 9), equal to -28/3. The bare value with no quotient does not earn the point.

Answers yes for 9 < t < 12, stating continuity on 9 <= t <= 12 and differentiability on 9 < t < 12 (or that A is differentiable) and invoking the Mean Value Theorem. An appeal to the Intermediate Value Theorem does not earn the point.

parts.prompt: Must there be a time \( t \), with \( 5 < t < 12 \), at which \( A'(t) = 0 \)? Justify your answer.

worked_solution.text: Average rate of change over 5 <= t <= 12. The endpoint altitudes are equal.
A is continuous on 5 <= t <= 12 and differentiable on 5 < t < 12, so the Mean Value Theorem (or Rolle's Theorem) gives such a time.

points.criterion: Shows (A(12) - A(5))/(12 - 5) = (62 - 62)/7 = 0, or states A(5) = A(12) = 62 as the equal endpoint values.

Answers yes, stating continuity on 5 <= t <= 12 and differentiability on 5 < t < 12 (or that A is differentiable) and invoking the Mean Value Theorem or Rolle's Theorem. An appeal to the Intermediate Value Theorem does not earn the point.

parts.prompt: Find the average rate of change of \( H \) over the interval \( 0 \le t \le 10 \). Must there be a time \( t \), with \( 0 < t < 10 \), at which \( H'(t) \) equals this average rate of change? Justify your answer.

worked_solution.text: Average rate of change of H over the interval.
H is linear on each side of t = 5.
worked_solution.latex: H'(t) = 4 \text{ for } 0 < t < 5, \quad H'(t) = -4 \text{ for } 5 < t < 10

worked_solution.text: H' is never 0, and H is not differentiable at t = 5, so the Mean Value Theorem does not apply and there is no such time.

points.criterion: Answers no, with the reason that H'(t) is 4 on 0 < t < 5 and -4 on 5 < t < 10 (and does not exist at t = 5), so H' never equals 0. Stating that the Mean Value Theorem does not apply because H is not differentiable at t = 5 is part of a complete answer. A yes answer, or a no supported only by the failed hypothesis with no check that H' is never 0, does not earn the point.
